picks.reasoning: Viper and Knight are simply better players than anything TLAW can put across from them, and I'm not backing off that just because the crowd likes BLG after the MKOI hiccup. CoreJJ is a real veteran who can drag a messy game sideways, and I'm rating that as skill, not chaos, but one great support doesn't outweigh a talent edge across the map, and the LPL-over-LCS gap points the same way.

usedLessons.text: Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but in a Bo1 I have to check whether the star's lane can actually turn that edge into a lead before I treat it as the whole argument. When the opposing team has a proven jungle-support duo that can steal a messy game, I should rate that duo as skill too, not dismiss it as chaos, and I should be more skeptical of a Viper-sized edge when the whole BLG team is the one the crowd is backing. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

Top lesson: One win doesn't prove my Chovy-over-Rookie call, because the debate showed GEN took early tempo and the map, not that Chovy won lane. Next time I'll back the side whose players are stronger across several roles, especially jungle and bot, since that's what builds early tempo, and not lean on a single marquee lane. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Top lesson: Individual skill still wins series, but I have to verify who has the stronger players on the actual rosters rather than assume the name on the jersey does. Keep judging the matchup player by player, leave region talk out unless the report flags a big gap, and ignore the "2-0 in their heads" vibes the crowd loves. (from Swiss G2 vs DK; picked DK, actual DK 1-0)

picks.thinking:

Given Viper and Knight likely carrying their lanes, with CoreJJ as the main threat to watch, I'm leaning toward BLG at roughly 65-66% probability despite their inconsistency and TLAW's strong lead-converting record.

picks.reasoning: Fast take: the region gap is huge, and I want it to show up as tempo. BLG's Jarvan and Pantheon jungle plus Viper and Lulu in the bot lane can turn the first herald and first dragon into towers before TLAW settles. TLAW's early game is real, though. Lee Sin or Pantheon skirmishes with CoreJJ roaming could steal the opening, and BLG just got burned at Worlds by exactly that kind of early chaos, so I'm trimming my confidence. If TLAW takes first herald and the first tower, I flip.

usedLessons.text: Jungle lesson: The early game still decides everything, so I should judge who wins the first fifteen minutes from the jungle matchup, the draft's early pressure and the first-objective setups, not from "better team" or region labels, which only count when the scouting report flags a big gap. When the other jungler can force early skirmishes, like Elyoya on Lee Sin, a Bo1 gives the favorite no time to recover, so I should cut my confidence instead of assuming they'll win tempo by default. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

Jungle lesson: I treated TLAW's early-tempo edge as a given when it was only a projection from Josedeodo's pathing. The first fifteen minutes still decide everything, but next time I'll check whether the opponent has early-game tools (e.g. CFO's Naafiri and Akali picks for early blood) that can contest the first dragons and tower, and drop my confidence when they do. I won't assume the "better" jungler wins that race by default. (from Swiss TLAW vs CFO; picked TLAW, actual CFO 1-0)

Jungle lesson: Tempo still decides games, so I should judge a team's first-15 pressure by what it shows against comparable opposition (jungle priority, first herald, first tower) instead of dismissing it as "built against CBLOL" or leaning on region records. I should treat region as a big factor only when the scouting report flags a BIG REGION GAP, and otherwise keep a clear flip trigger like "LOS take early jungle priority and first herald" and let the early map decide. (from Swiss LOS vs T1; picked T1, actual T1 1-0)

Jungle lesson: The early game still decides everything, so when a big region gap is flagged, I should confirm it shows up as first-15-minute tempo (jungle pathing, lane priority, first objectives) and not lean on star names or records. I can also borrow Mid's draft point: a deep draft is what hands you that early priority, so I'll check whether a team's picks set up the first tower and dragon before I raise my confidence. picks.thinking:

TLAW actually shows better early-game numbers though—higher gold lead at 15, better first tower and first dragon rates than BLG, suggesting they might outpace BLG's historically stronger LCS competition despite the region gap.

Checking jungle matchups, both sides run aggressive early-skirmish champions—BLG with Jarvan/Pantheon/Naafiri, TLAW with Pantheon/Lee Sin/Qiyana—so there's real contest potential for Pantheon and tempo control. Given BLG's Worlds loss showed a significant early deficit while TLAW stayed competitive before falling, I'm leaning BLG but tempering confidence since TLAW's jungle tools could flip the early skirmish picture if they secure first herald or drake.

picks.reasoning: My draft-first read lands on BLG: the Yunara/Lulu lane pair is a comfort pick Fearless can't easily strip, and Viper gives them a carry who closes games once Jarvan or Pantheon sets the tempo. TLAW can win by taking early priority with Pantheon or Lee Sin and getting Yeon on Jhin, with CoreJJ's peel on top. But the region gap is flagged as a very big factor this time, so I'll back BLG, and the first-pick fight over Yunara or Pantheon is what would swing me.

usedLessons.text: Mid lesson: Pool depth only matters if it shows up in the draft, and in a Bo1 a team's few comfort picks (like MKOI's Ryze and Lee Sin) can beat a broader pool, so I should judge how each side's best picks match up instead of counting champions. When the upset path I name is built on the opponent's comfort picks, I should cut my confidence until the draft shows BLG can deny or punish them, and not lean on league strength unless the report flags a big gap. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

usedLessons.text: ADC lesson: When a team's headline record and its away or cross-region record diverge sharply (TSW's 16-4 versus 1-6 outside the LCP), trust the split that matches the matchup. ADC lesson: Numbers over stories means weighing how much each number can actually predict, and in a Bo1 a 125-52 season record and one EWC win are a thin edge, so I shouldn't have put 76 on them. Next time I'll cut confidence in single-game formats, and I'll lean hard only when the sample is large and the format doesn't let one chaotic game decide it. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

ADC lesson: A single 1-0 in a Bo1 is one data point and doesn't validate a 71% call, so I should judge myself on whether the numbers (the 6-1 vs 0-2 international records and the flagged big region gap) justified that confidence, not on the result. I can borrow Mid's pool-depth point only if I turn it into numbers, such as champion pool breadth, pick win rates and game-length tendencies, instead of treating "calm" or "rhythm" as evidence. (from Swiss HLE vs TES; picked HLE, actual HLE 1-0)

ADC lesson: A record like "nine for nine on 15-minute leads" only tells me what happens after a lead exists, so I should check how often a team actually gets that lead before treating the number as a reason to pick them. Numbers over stories means asking whether a stat applies to the matchup in front of me, and in a coinflip-length best of 1 I should keep confidence near even when the decisive stat is conditional. But BLG are an 0-1 side with a veteran core, Viper to lean on, and a lot to prove after the MSI final heartbreak. They can play loose and together here, and when the region gap is this big I won't let a lovely locker room drag me off them, though if BLG start crumbling after another lost lead, TLAW's calm could take the series.

usedLessons.text: Support lesson: I read BLG's chemistry as a strength and MKOI's youth as fragility, but a team that has been blown out internationally and has nothing to lose can play loose and unified, so I should weigh how a team's mood actually shows up in its recent games rather than leaning on a narrative like "hungry after an MSI final" or "young and shaky." Next time I'll ask which room is more settled and free right now, and treat the "if they fall behind" wobble as a risk on both sides, not just the underdog's. (from Swiss BLG vs MKOI; picked BLG, actual MKOI 1-0)

Support lesson: I was right that HLE's calm mattered, but I leaned on "mood" without checking it against what the team actually did, so next time I'll look for chemistry in concrete signs like coordinated early pressure, turning leads into towers and dragons, and a draft the whole team clearly bought into. I'll also remember that a team's morale tends to show in how cleanly they convert advantages, and I won't treat TES's "wobbling" as proof of low morale unless I can point to specific evidence. (from Swiss HLE vs TES; picked HLE, actual HLE 1-0)

Support lesson: Team chemistry decides games, but I should anchor that read in things I can see, like comebacks, composure after setbacks, and clean early-game coordination (GEN's tempo is where "locked-in" actually showed up), rather than claiming the vibes were obvious afterward. I should also bring in region only when the scouting report flags a big gap, and otherwise let the team's mood and cohesion carry the pick. (from Swiss GEN vs IG; picked GEN, actual GEN 1-0)

Support lesson: When I read a team's chemistry and morale, I should weigh what I see in the actual game against my read of their character. CFO's past collapses were evidence about their mood, but the chemistry call only holds if I also check the current signals, like roster stability, how they were playing lately, and whether those lead-throwing games were still shaping their confidence. I'll keep trusting that the team decides it, but I'll hold my read of a side's nerves more loosely and lower my confidence when the story I'm telling is one every other analyst also tells. (from Swiss TLAW vs CFO; picked TLAW, actual CFO 1-0)

picks.thinking:
I'm weighing the region strength factor heavily—LPL looks stronger than LCS—but noting both teams already have a Worlds loss in Swiss stage, so that gap alone shouldn't decide things without more context.

Looking at chemistry signals: TLAW has CoreJJ steadying things with a strong comeback record and no recent throws, riding a hot streak, while BLG has dropped two straight and blown leads, including the tough loss to MKOI. Still, the region gap rule says I need clear international results to override it, and TLAW's international record (2-3, 0-1 at Worlds) isn't convincing enough compared to BLG's much stronger 8-3 mark, so I'm leaning toward picking BLG on that basis.
